# 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Topic and Event Description

- Main topic: CONTROL Resonant
- Specific event: Release Day of CONTROL Resonant
- Event date: 24 September 2026
- Selected subtopic: Gameplay and Combat
- Data source: Bluesky
- Data collection period: Before event (17/09/2026 - 23/09/2026) and After event (25/09/2026 - 01/10/2026)

## 1.2 Research Objectives

- Objective 1: Investigate changes in discussion volume and subtopic proportions.
- Objective 2: Identify discussion themes through text mining.
- Objective 3: Discover comment clusters and their relationships with discussion threads.
- Objective 4: Investigate the interaction network of active users.

# 2. Question 1: Trend & Time Series Analysis

## Collect and clean dataset

```{r}
# 1. Set the event date and collection periods
event_date <- as.Date("2026-09-24")

# Take the same equal period of 7 days for before and after the event
before_start <- event_date - 7
before_end <- event_date - 1

after_start <- event_date + 1
after_end <- event_date + 7

# Display the selected dates
cat("Before period:", as.character(before_start), 
    "to", as.character(before_end), "\n")

cat("Event day:", as.character(event_date), "\n")

cat("After period:", as.character(after_start),
    "to", as.character(after_end), "\n")

# 2. Create a folder to save data
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

# 3. Collect data
# Collect posts BEFORE the event day
before_raw <- search_post(
  q = "CONTROL Resonant",
  since = as.character(before_start),
  until = as.character(before_end + 1),
  limit = 5000
)

before_raw$period <- "Before"
cat("Before:", nrow(before_raw), "posts\n")

# Collect posts ON the event day
event_raw <- search_post(
  q = "CONTROL Resonant",
  since = as.character(event_date),
  until = as.character(event_date + 1),
  limit = 5000
)

event_raw$period <- "Event day"
cat("Event day:", nrow(event_raw), "posts\n")

# Collect posts AFTER the event
after_raw <- search_post(
  q = "CONTROL Resonant",
  since = as.character(after_start),
  until = as.character(after_end + 1),
  limit = 5000
)

after_raw$period <- "After"
cat("After:", nrow(after_raw), "posts\n")

# 4. Clean data by date period
# Filter posts to the intended date ranges
before_clean <- before_raw %>%
  mutate(post_date = as.Date(created_at)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(post_date),
    post_date >= before_start,
    post_date <= before_end)

event_clean <- event_raw %>%
  mutate(post_date = as.Date(created_at)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(post_date),
    post_date == event_date)

after_clean <- after_raw %>%
  mutate(post_date = as.Date(created_at)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(post_date),
    post_date >= after_start,
    post_date <= after_end)

# Remove duplicate posts using their URI
before_clean <- before_clean %>%
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE)

event_clean <- event_clean %>%
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE)

after_clean <- after_clean %>%
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Assign period labels
before_clean <- before_clean %>%
  mutate(period = "Before")

event_clean <- event_clean %>%
  mutate(period = "Event")

after_clean <- after_clean %>%
  mutate(period = "After")

# Count posts without readable text
count_no_text <- function(data) {
  sum(is.na(data$text) | trimws(data$text) == "")
}

before_no_text <- count_no_text(before_clean)
event_no_text <- count_no_text(event_clean)
after_no_text <- count_no_text(after_clean)

cat("Before posts without text:", count_no_text(before_clean), "\n")
cat("Event posts without text:", count_no_text(event_clean), "\n")
cat("After posts without text:", count_no_text(after_clean), "\n")

# Select the columns needed for analysis
before_export <- before_clean %>%
  select(
    uri, cid, author_handle, author_name, text,
    reply_count, repost_count, like_count,
    created_at, post_date, period,
    in_reply_to, in_reply_root
  )

event_export <- event_clean %>%
  select(
    uri, cid, author_handle, author_name, text,
    reply_count, repost_count, like_count,
    created_at, post_date, period,
    in_reply_to, in_reply_root
  )

after_export <- after_clean %>%
  select(
    uri, cid, author_handle, author_name, text,
    reply_count, repost_count, like_count,
    created_at, post_date, period,
    in_reply_to, in_reply_root
  )

analysis_export <- bind_rows(before_export, after_export)
```

## Export the cleaned dataset for further analysis

```{r}

write.csv(event_export, "data/event_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(after_export, "data/after_event.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Question 1A: Classify the subtopic

### 1. Load the analysis dataset and classify data without text

```{r}
# Prepare data for subtopic classification
classification_data <- analysis_export %>%
  filter(!is.na(text), trimws(text) != "")

# Check the number of posts available for classification by period
cat("Original posts:", nrow(analysis_export), "\n")
cat("Readale posts:", nrow(classification_data), "\n")
cat("Excluded posts:", 
    nrow(analysis_export) - nrow(classification_data), "\n")

# Check the number of posts for each period
classification_data %>%
  count(period)
```

### 2. Define subtopic and inclusion/exclusion rules

- The selected subtopic is Gameplay and Combat in CONTROL Resonant.
- For subtopic classification, this part focuses on examining posts that discuss the game's gameplay and combat systems, weapons, abilities, boss encounters, movement, controls, and overall gameplay experience.

**Inclusion and Exclusion Rules**

- Before subtopic classification, all non-readable posts is excluded in classification_data. Therefore, in this part, posts is classified into Subtopic and No-Subtopic. The classification rules is followed below:

- Subtopic is explicitly discusses at least one aspect of Gameplay and Combat.

- No-Subtopic does not explicitly discuss Gameplay and Combat.

**Subtopic Content Included:**

- Combat systems and mechanics

- Weapons and fighting styles

- Abilities, skills and combos

- Boss encounters and difficulty

- Movement and player controls

- Exploration and gameplay experience, when explicitly discussed as gameplay

**Brief methodology:** To identify and classify posts related to the Gameplay and Combat subtopic, a multi-step process was conducted.

- First, a reference sample of 200 posts (100 Before and 100 After) was prepared. Based on the gameplay_keywords, the reference sample was firstly labelled TRUE or FALSE on the has_keyword variable and then was manually labelled and assign Subtopic or No-Subtopic on the manual_label variable. This reference sample was established to provide example of Subtopic and No-Subtopic posts for further steps.

- Secondly, TF-IDF was then used to transform the text into numerical vectors, while Cosine Similarity measured the similarity between posts to support the classification process.

- Posts that could not be confidently classified were subsequently reviewed manually before combining the results into the final labelled dataset.

### 3. Identify potential Gameplay and Combat posts

```{r}
# Define Gameplay and Combat keywords
gameplay_keywords <- paste(
  "gameplay",
  "combat",
  "fight",
  "fighting",
  "weapon",
  "abiity",
  "abilities",
  "skill",
  "skills",
  "combo",
  "boss",
  "attack",
  "movement",
  "mechanic",
  "mechanics",
  "exploration",
  "parry",
  "dodge",
  "melee",
  "traversal",
  "controls",
  sep = "|"
)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Randomly sample 200 posts: 100 Before + 100 After
set.seed(2026)

reference_sample <- classification_data %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 100) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    has_keyword = str_detect(
      text,
      regex(gameplay_keywords, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    sample_id = row_number(),
    manual_label = NA_character_
  ) %>%
  select(sample_id, period, has_keyword, manual_label, text)

# Check sample distribution
reference_sample %>%
  count(period, has_keyword)

# Open the 200 posts for manual review
View(reference_sample)

# Save the reference sample
write.csv(
  reference_sample,
  "data/reference_sample_200.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
# Import the manually labelled reference sample to preserve the human annotations and ensure consistent classification results when knitting the report
reference_sample <- read.csv(
  "data/reference_sample_200.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

# Check manual labels 
table(reference_sample$manual_label, useNA = "ifany")

stopifnot(!any(is.na(reference_sample$manual_label)))
```

### 4. Create a matching key and prepare reference and unlabelled data

```{r}
# Create a matching key using period and key
reference_sample <- reference_sample %>%
  mutate(match_key = paste(period, text, sep = "|||"))

classification_data <- classification_data %>%
  mutate(match_key = paste(period, text, sep = "|||"))

# Create a normalized text-to-URI mapping
reference_uri_map <- classification_data %>%
  mutate(text_norm = str_squish(text)) %>%
  group_by(period, text_norm) %>%
  summarize(
    uri = first(uri), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Keep exactly 200 manually labelled reference posts
reference_data <- reference_sample %>%
  mutate(
    text_norm = str_squish(text),
    doc_id = paste0("ref_", sample_id)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    reference_uri_map,
    by = c("period", "text_norm")
  )

# Identify reference URIs
reference_uris <- reference_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(uri)) %>%
  distinct(uri)

# Remove reference posts from unlabelled dataset
unlabelled_data <- classification_data %>%
  anti_join(
    reference_uris, by = "uri") %>%
    mutate(doc_id = paste0("post_", row_number()))

# Check dataset sizes
cat("Reference posts", nrow(reference_data), "\n")
cat("Unique reference URIs:", nrow(reference_uris), "\n")
cat("Posts to classify:", nrow(unlabelled_data), "\n")
cat("Total combined posts:",
    nrow(reference_data) + nrow(unlabelled_data), "\n")
```

### 5. Calculate TF-IDF

```{r}
# Combine reference and unlabelled data
combined_data <- bind_rows(
  reference_data %>%
    select(doc_id, period, text, manual_label),
  unlabelled_data %>%
    mutate(manual_label = NA_character_) %>%
    select(doc_id, period, text, manual_label)
)

# Tokenization - split text into individual words
tokens_data <- combined_data %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

# Remove common words (stop words)
tokens_data <- tokens_data %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

# Calculate TF-IDF
tfidf_data <- tokens_data %>%
  count(doc_id, word, name = "n") %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = doc_id,
    n = n
  )

# Check the results
head(tfidf_data)

cat("Total documents:", n_distinct(tfidf_data$doc_id), "\n")
cat("Total unique words:", n_distinct(tfidf_data$word), "\n")

# Convert TF-IDF data into a document-term matrix
tfidf_matrix <- tfidf_data %>%
  select(doc_id, word, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = word,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# Convert to matrix
tfidf_matrix_numeric <- as.matrix(
  tfidf_matrix %>%
    select(-doc_id)
)

# Set document IDs as row names
rownames(tfidf_matrix_numeric) <- tfidf_matrix$doc_id

# Check dimensions
dim(tfidf_matrix_numeric)
```

### 6. Calculate Cosine Similarity

```{r}
# Separate reference and unlabelled documents
reference_ids <- reference_data$doc_id
unlabelled_ids <- unlabelled_data$doc_id

# Keep only documents that exist in the TF-IDF matrix
reference_ids <- intersect(reference_ids, rownames(tfidf_matrix_numeric))
unlabelled_ids <- intersect(unlabelled_ids, rownames(tfidf_matrix_numeric))

reference_matrix <- tfidf_matrix_numeric[
  reference_ids, , drop = FALSE
]
unlabelled_matrix <- tfidf_matrix_numeric[
  unlabelled_ids, , drop = FALSE
]

# Calculate cosine similarity using matrix multiplication

# Calculate dot product
similarity_matrix <- unlabelled_matrix %*% t(reference_matrix)

# Calculate vector magnitudes
row_norms <- sqrt(rowSums(unlabelled_matrix^2))
col_norms <- sqrt(rowSums(reference_matrix^2))

# Calculate cosine similarity
denominator <- outer(row_norms, col_norms)

similarity_matrix <- similarity_matrix / denominator

# Handle invalid values and assign matrix labels
similarity_matrix[!is.finite(similarity_matrix)] <- 0

rownames(similarity_matrix) <- rownames(unlabelled_matrix)
colnames(similarity_matrix) <- rownames(reference_matrix)

# Check similarity matrix
dim(similarity_matrix)
```

### 7. Calculate average of top 3 similarities by class

```{r}
# Identify reference labels
reference_labels <- reference_data$manual_label[
  match(colnames(similarity_matrix), reference_data$doc_id)
]

# Identify reference groups
subtopic_index <- which(reference_labels == "Subtopic")
no_subtopic_index <- which(reference_labels == "No-Subtopic")

# Calculate mean of the top 3 similarity scores
top3_mean <- function(x) {
  mean(sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3])
}

subtopic_similarity <- apply(
  similarity_matrix[, subtopic_index, drop = FALSE],
  1,
  top3_mean
)

no_subtopic_similarity <- apply(
  similarity_matrix[, no_subtopic_index, drop = FALSE],
  1,
  top3_mean
)
```

### 8. Create classification suggestions

#### 8.1 Generate automatic classification suggestions

```{r}
classification_suggestions <- unlabelled_data %>%
  filter(doc_id %in% rownames(similarity_matrix)) %>%
  mutate(
    subtopic_similarity = subtopic_similarity[doc_id],
    no_subtopic_similarity = no_subtopic_similarity[doc_id],
    similarity_gap = abs(
      subtopic_similarity - no_subtopic_similarity
    ),
    suggested_label = case_when(
      subtopic_similarity > no_subtopic_similarity ~ "Subtopic",
      no_subtopic_similarity > subtopic_similarity ~ "No-Subtopic",
      TRUE ~ "Needs manual review"
    )
  )

summary(classification_suggestions$subtopic_similarity)
summary(classification_suggestions$no_subtopic_similarity)
head(classification_suggestions %>%
       select(doc_id, subtopic_similarity,
              no_subtopic_similarity), 10)
table(classification_suggestions$suggested_label)
```

#### 8.2 Export posts for manual review

```{r, eval=FALSE}
manual_review <- classification_suggestions %>%
  filter(
    subtopic_similarity == 0 &
    no_subtopic_similarity == 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    suggested_label = "Needs manual review",
    manual_label = NA_character_
  ) %>%
  select(
    doc_id,
    period,
    text,
    subtopic_similarity,
    no_subtopic_similarity,
    similarity_gap,
    manual_label
  )
```

#### 8.3 Export CSV file for manual labels

```{r, eval =FALSE}
write.csv(
  manual_review,
  "manual_review_posts.csv",
  row.names = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
```

## Question 1B: Chi-Square Test of Independence

**State the hypothesis**

- H0 (Null Hypothesis): The subtopic status is independent of time period.

- H1 (Alternative Hypothesis): The subtopic status is associated with time period.

### 1. Create a contingency table

```{r}
classification_table <- table(
  Period = classification_final$period,
  Subtopic_Status = classification_final$final_label
)

classification_table
```

### 2. Chi-square test

```{r}
# Perform Chi-square test of independence
chi_result <- chisq.test(
  classification_table,
  correct = FALSE
)

# View the Chi-square result
print(chi_result)

print(chi_result$expected)
```

**Conclusion:** Since the p_value (0.015) \< alpha (0.05), the null hypothesis (H0) is rejected. Additionally, all expected cell counts exceeded 5, satisfying the commonly use expected-frequency guideline for the test. Therefore, the subtopic status is associated with the time period. However, the association does not establish that the release itself caused the increase.

## Question 1C: Comparison of Chi-square score

**Purpose of the analysis**

- In Question 1C, it examines whether the proportion of subtopic posts changed from the "Before" (past) period to the "After" (current) period, by calculating Bluesky's Chi-square score.

**Baseline**

- The baseline is the proportion of Gameplay and Combat posts among all CONTROL Resonant posts collected during the Before period (Past).

- The Past proportion is also used to calculate the expected number of Gameplay and Combat posts in the Current period.

**Denominator**

- Np: The total number of CONTROL Resonant posts collected during the Past period (Before).

- X: The number of Gameplay and Combat posts collected during the Past period (Before).

- Nc: The total number of CONTROL Resonant posts collected during the Current period (After).

- Y: The number of Gameplay and Combat posts collected during the current period (After).

- The denominator for each period includes all CONTROL Resonant posts, consisting of both Subtopic posts and No-Subtopic posts.

- The proportion of Gameplay and Combat posts in each period is calculated as:

pPast = X/Np

pCurrent = Y/Nc

### 1. Prepare dataset

```{r}
# 1.1 Add post dates to the final classification dataset
post_dates <- classification_data %>%
  select(uri, post_date) %>%
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE)

# 1.2 Combine all document IDs and URIs
q1c_data <- bind_rows(
  reference_data %>% select(doc_id, uri),
  unlabelled_classification_final %>% select(doc_id, uri),
  posts_without_tfidf_final %>% select(doc_id, uri)
) %>%
  left_join(post_dates, by = "uri") %>%
  left_join(
    classification_final %>% select(doc_id, final_label),
    by = "doc_id"
  )

# 1.3 Check the dataset
nrow(q1c_data)

# Check duplicate document IDs
sum(duplicated(q1c_data$doc_id))

# Check missing post dates
sum(is.na(q1c_data$post_date))

# Check the posts without post dates
q1c_data %>%
  filter(is.na(post_date)) %>%
  select(doc_id, final_label, post_date)

# Check post date distribution
table(q1c_data$post_date)

# Check classification distribution
table(q1c_data$final_label, useNA = "ifany")


```

### 2. Separate Past and Current periods

```{r}
# 2.1 Classify posts into Past and Current periods
q1c_data <- q1c_data %>%
  mutate(
    post_date = as.Date(post_date),
    period = case_when(
      post_date >= as.Date("2026-09-17") &
        post_date <= as.Date("2026-09-23") ~ "Past",
      
      post_date >= as.Date("2026-09-25") &
        post_date <= as.Date("2026-10-01") ~ "Current",
      
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

# 2.2 Keep only posts within the two analysis periods
q1c_data <- q1c_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(period))

# 2.3 Check the period distribution

# Check the number of posts in each period
table(q1c_data$period)

# Check the number of posts by date and period
table(q1c_data$post_date, q1c_data$period)

# Check the classification distribution by period
table(q1c_data$period, q1c_data$final_label)
```

### 3. Create a contingency table

```{r}
# 3.1 Create the contingency table
q1c_table <- table(
  factor(q1c_data$period, levels = c("Past", "Current")),
  factor(q1c_data$final_label,
         levels = c("Subtopic", "No-Subtopic"))
)

# 3.2 Display the contingency table
q1c_table

# 3.3 Calculate the total number of posts in each period
rowSums(q1c_table)

# 3.4 Calculate the total number of posts in each classification
colSums(q1c_table)

# 3.5 Calculate the proportion of Gameplay and Combat posts
round(
  q1c_table[, "Subtopic"] / rowSums(q1c_table) * 100,
  2
)
```

### 4. Calculate Bluesky's Chi-square score

```{r}
# 4.1 Extract observed counts from the contingency table
Np <- sum(q1c_table["Past", ])
X <- q1c_table["Past", "Subtopic"]

Nc <- sum(q1c_table["Current", ])
Y <- q1c_table["Current", "Subtopic"]

# Display observed counts
Np
X
Nc
Y

# 4.2 Calculate the baseline and current proportions
p_past <- X / Np
p_current <- Y / Nc

p_past
p_current

# 4.2 Calculate expected frequencies for Current
E_subtopic <- Nc * p_past
E_nosubtopic <- Nc - E_subtopic

# Display expected frequencies
E_subtopic
E_nosubtopic

# 4.4 Calculate Bluesky's Chi-square score
bluesky_chisquare <-
  ((Y - E_subtopic) ^ 2 / E_subtopic) +
  ((Nc - Y - E_nosubtopic) ^ 2 / E_nosubtopic)

# Display the final result
bluesky_chisquare
```

**Conclusion**

- The proportion of Gameplay and Combat posts increased from 4.00% in the Past period to 5.26% in the Current period, indicating an increase of approximately 1.26%.

- Based on the Past-period proportion, 193.21 Subtopic posts were expected in the Current period, whereas 254 was observed.

- The resulting Bluesky's Chi-square score was 19.93, illustrating a noticeable deviation from the baseline in the Past period.

- These findings suggest that Gameplay and Combat discussions became more prevalent during the Current period.

**Explain why the two Chi-square scores different**

- The two Chi-square scores differ because they use different methods to calculate the expected frequencies.

- In Question 1B, Pearson's Chi-square test of independence calculates expected frequencies based on the row and column totals of the entire contingency table. The Chi-square statistic was 5.917 (p = 0.015).

- In Question 1C, it calculates Bluesky's Chi-square score by using the Subtopic proportion in the Past period as the baseline. This baseline proportion (4.00%) is used to calculate the expected number of Subtopic posts in the Current period. While the expected number was 193.21, the observed number was 254, resulting in a Chi-square score of 19.93.

- Consequently, although both calculations use the same observed dataset, they produce different scores because their expected frequencies are calculated differently.

## Question 1D: Simple Linear Regression

### 1. Calculate daily post counts

```{r}
daily_counts <- analysis_export %>%
  group_by(post_date) %>%
  summarize(
    Total_Posts = n()
  ) %>%
  arrange(post_date)

# Convert post date to Date format and create time variable
daily_counts <- daily_counts %>%
  mutate(
    post_date = as.Date(post_date),
    time = as.numeric(post_date - min(post_date))
  )

# Display daily post counts
print(daily_counts, n = Inf)
```

### 2. Fit a simple linear regression model

```{r}
regression_model <- lm(Total_Posts ~ time, data = daily_counts)

# Display regression results
summary(regression_model)

# Extract key statistics
slope <- coef(regression_model)[["time"]]
print(slope)

r_squared <- summary(regression_model)$r.squared
print(r_squared)
```

### 3. Visualize daily post counts and regression line using a scatter plot

```{r}
regression_plot <- ggplot(daily_counts, aes(x = time, y = Total_Posts)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily CONTROL Resonant Posts Over Time",
    x = "Days Since 17 September 2026",
    y = "Number of Posts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Display the plot
print(regression_plot)

# Save the plot
ggsave(
  "q1d_daily_post_regression.png",
  plot = regression_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

**Interpretation the slope and R-squared:**

- The slope is 28.52 indicates that the predicted number of posts increased by approximately 28.52 posts per day.

- The R-squared value of 0.3461 indicates that time explains approximately 34.61% of the variation in daily posts counts, while the remaining 65.39% is unexplained by the linear model. Although the positive slope is statistically significant (p-value = 0.02691), the scatter plot shows considerable day-to-day fluctuations, with some sharp increases and decreases.

- Therefore, the model suggests a positive linear trend overall, but the relationship is not strongly linear, and time alone does not adequately explain the chnages in daily post activity.

## Question 1E: Limitations of the Linear Trend

Linear regression has several limitations when analyzing viral spikes in Social Web data.

1.  It assumes a linear regression between time and post counts, which may not accurately represent sudden increases or decreases in online activity.

2.  Viral spikes can cause extreme fluctuations in daily post counts. Meanwhile, a straight regression line cannot capture these sudden increases and subsequent declines.

3.  The model only considers time as an explanatory variable and does not account for other factors that may influence posting activity, such as trending discussions, user engagement, or external events.

Therefore, although linear regression can illustrate the overall trend, it may not be suitable for accurately predicting sudden viral spikes or short-term fluctuations in Social Web activity.

```{r}
      direct_replies = sum(

        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
      # Nested replies: Posts that respond to other replies within the thread
      nested_replies = sum(
        !is.na(thread$in_reply_to) &
          thread$in_reply_to != root_uri
      ),
      # Total replies: The sum of direct and nested replies.

      reported_reply_count = top3_posts$reply_count[i]

  })

thread_summary
```

# Question 3: Clustering & Visualization

## Question 3A: Data Preparation and TF-IDF

### 1. Combine all discussion threads

```{r}
all_comments <- bind_rows(
  lapply(seq_along(discussion_threads), function(i) {
    discussion_threads[[i]] %>%
      mutate(thread = paste0("Thread ", i))
  })
)
```

### 2. Text Pre-processing

```{r}
# Keep replies only and select required columns
all_comments <- all_comments %>%
  filter(!is.na(in_reply_to)) %>%
  select(thread, uri, text)

# Remove missing and empty comments
all_comments_clean <- all_comments %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(text),
    trimws(text) != ""
  )

# Check and save cleaned dataset
dim(all_comments_clean)
table(all_comments_clean$thread)

write.csv(
  all_comments_clean,
  "q3a_all_comments_clean.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Tokenization - Convert comments into individual words
comments_tokens <- all_comments_clean %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

# Remove stop words and short words
comments_clean <- comments_tokens %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(str_length(word) >= 2)
```

### 3. Calculate TF-IDF

```{r}
# Assign each comment a document ID
comments_clean <- comments_clean %>%
  mutate(document_id = uri)

# Count term frequency in each document
term_frequency <- comments_clean %>%
  count(document_id, word, name = "tf")

# Calculate TF-IDF
tfidf_data_q3a <- term_frequency %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = document_id,
    n = tf
  )
```

### 4. Construct TF-IDF Document-Term Matrix

```{r}
dtm_tfidf_q3a <- tfidf_data_q3a %>%
  select(document_id, word, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = word,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# Convert to numeric matrix
dtm_tfidf_numeric_q3a <- as.matrix(
  dtm_tfidf_q3a %>%
    select(-document_id)
)

# Keep thread labels for subsequent analysis
document_info_q3a <- dtm_tfidf_q3a %>%
  select(document_id) %>%
  left_join(
    comments_clean %>%
      distinct(document_id, thread),
    by = "document_id"
  )

# Check final DTM
dim(dtm_tfidf_numeric_q3a)
```

## Question 3B: Determine Optimal Number of Clusters

**Method Selection**

- The Silhouette Method was used to determine the optimal number of clusters for the TF-IDF document-term matrix. The number of clusters (K) was tested from 2 to 10 using K-means clustering.

- The Average Silhouette Width was calculated for each value of K to evaluate intra-cluster cohension and inter-cluster separation. A higher score indicates better clustering quality.

### 1. Calculate Euclidean distance

```{r}
distance_matrix <- dist(dtm_tfidf_numeric_q3a)
```

### 2. Calculate Average Silhouette Width for each K

```{r}
set.seed(123) # set random seed for reproducibility

# Define the range of K values
k_values <- 2:10
silhouette_results <- data.frame()

# Test different numbers of clusters
for (k in k_values) {
  
  # Apply K-means
  km <- kmeans(
    dtm_tfidf_numeric_q3a,
    centers = k,
    nstart = 25,
    iter.max = 100
  )
  
  # Calculate Silhouette Width for this K
  sil <- silhouette(
    km$cluster,
    distance_matrix
  )
  
  # Calculate Average Silhouette Width
  avg_sil <- mean(sil[, "sil_width"])
  
  silhouette_results <- rbind(
    silhouette_results,
    data.frame(
      K = k,
      Average_Silhouette_Width = avg_sil
    )
  )
}

# Display results
print(silhouette_results)
```

### 3. Identify optimal K

```{r}
optimal_k <- silhouette_results$K[
  which.max(silhouette_results$Average_Silhouette_Width)
]

print(optimal_k)
```

### 4. Visualize Silhouette Scores

```{r}
plot(
  silhouette_results$K,
  silhouette_results$Average_Silhouette_Width,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  xlab = "Number of Clusters (K)",
  ylab = "Average Silhouette Width",
  main = "Silhouette Method for Choosing K"
)
```

**Result:** The results showed that K = 5 achieved the highest Average Silhouette Width of 0.4333. Although the score for K = 2 to K = 5 were relatively similar, the score decreased considerably when K exceeded 5.

Therefore, K = 5 was selected as the optimal number of clusters based on the highest Average Silhouette Width.

## Question 3C: Apply Clustering Technique

**Clustering Method: K-means**

- Compatibility with numerical data: TF-IDF converts comments into numerical vectors. K-means can utilize these vectors to calculate distances and perform clustering.

- Alignment with clustering objectives: The goal is to group comments with similar content into the same cluster. K-means achieve this by minimizing the sum of squared distances from data points to the centroid of their respective cluster (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares).

- Predefined number of clusters: We employed the Silhouette Method in Q3B and determined that K = 5. K-means allows for the specification of the number of clusters in advance via the cluster centers.

**Explain Parameter Choices**

- centers = 5: Divide comments into 5 clusters, following the optimal number of clusters identified in Question 3B.

- nstart = 25: Performs 25 different centroid initializations to find a better solution.

- iter.max = 100: Sets a maximum limit on the number of iterations.

- set.seed(123): Ensures the results can be replicated when the code is run again.

### 1. Apply K-means clustering

```{r}
# Set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Perform K-means clustering
kmeans_result_q3c <- kmeans(
  dtm_tfidf_numeric_q3a,
      centers = 5,
      nstart = 25,
      iter.max = 100
)
```

### 2. Display the number of comments in each cluster

```{r}
cluster_sizes <- table(kmeans_result_q3c$cluster)
print(cluster_sizes)
```

### 3. Evaluate clustering results

```{r}
clustering_evaluation <- data.frame(
  Total_Within_SS = kmeans_result_q3c$tot.withinss,
  Between_SS = kmeans_result_q3c$betweenss,
  Total_SS = kmeans_result_q3c$totss,
  Between_SS_Ration = kmeans_result_q3c$betweenss /
    kmeans_result_q3c$totss
)

print(clustering_evaluation)
```

### 4. Combine cluster assignments with original thread labels

```{r}
clustered_comments_q3c <- document_info_q3a %>%
  mutate(
    cluster = factor(kmeans_result_q3c$cluster)
  )

# View the results
head(clustered_comments_q3c)
```

**Conclusion** The K-means algorithm produced six clusters, although the cluster sizes were highly uneven. The largest cluster contained 202 comments, while the remaining clusters contained 11, 1, 1, and 1 comments, respectively. Further inspections showed that comments in the smaller clusters were generally very short, consisting of only 1-8 words. These comments may have distinctive TF-IDF representations compared with the majority of comments. This suggests that the clustering result may partly reflect differences in comment characteristics rather than clearly separated discussion topics.

# Question 4: Network Analysis (Bluesky)

## Question 4A: Identify the Three Most Active Users

### 1. Count posts by each user

```{r}
user_ranking <- analysis_export %>%
  group_by(author_handle) %>%
  summarize(
    post_count = n(),
    author_did = first(sub( # retrieve and save DID from each post's URI
      "^at://([^/]+)/.*$",
      "\\1",
      uri
    )),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(post_count))
```

### 2. Display Top 3 users

```{r}
top3_users <- head(user_ranking, 3)

print(top3_users)

# Export Top 3 users
write.csv(
  top3_users,
  "q4a_top3_users.csv",
   row.names = FALSE
)
```

## Question 4B: Retrieve Followers and Following

### 1. Collect followers and following

```{r}
# Create empty lists to store API results
followers_list <- list()
following_list <- list()

# Loop through the Top 3 users
for (i in seq_len(nrow(top3_users))) {
  
  # Get current user's information
  current_did <- top3_users$author_did[i]
  current_handle <- top3_users$author_handle[i]
  
  message("Collecting network for: ", current_handle)
  
  # 1.1 Get followers
  current_followers <- tryCatch(
    atrrr::get_followers(
      actor = current_did,
      limit = 50
    ), 
    error = function(e) {
      message("Error retrieving followers: ", e$message)
      NULL
    }
  )
  
  # Keep maximum 50 followers
  if (!is.null(current_followers) && nrow(current_followers) > 0) {
    
    current_followers <- current_followers %>%
      slice_head(n = 50) %>%
      mutate(
        target_user_did = current_did,
        target_user_handle = current_handle
      )
    
    followers_list[[i]] <- current_followers
  } else {
    followers_list[[i]] <- tibble
  }
  
  # 1.2 Get following accounts
  current_following <- tryCatch(
    atrrr::get_follows(
      actor = current_did,
      limit = 50
    ),
    error = function(e) {
      message("Error retrieving following: ", e$message)
      NULL
    }
  )
  
  # Keep maximum 50 following accounts
  if(!is.null(current_following) && nrow(current_following) > 0) {
    
    current_following <- current_following %>%
      slice_head(n = 50) %>%
      mutate(
        source_user_did = current_did,
        source_user_handle = current_handle
      )
    
    following_list[[i]] <- current_following
  } else {
    following_list[[i]] <- tibble()
  }
  
  # Short pause between users
  Sys.sleep(1)
}

# 1.3 Combine results from all 3 users
all_followers <- bind_rows(followers_list)
all_following <- bind_rows(following_list)

# 1.4 Inspect collection results
cat("\nTotal followers:", nrow(all_followers), "\n")
cat("Total following:", nrow(all_following), "\n")

# 1.5 Check number of records for each selected user
print(
  all_followers %>%
    count(target_user_handle, name = "follower_count")
)

print(
  all_following %>%
    count(source_user_handle, name = "following_count")
)
```

### 2. Create network edge list

```{r}
# 2.1 Create edges from followers to selected users
edges_from_followers <- all_followers %>%
  transmute(
    from_did = did,
    to_did = target_user_did,
    from_handle = actor_handle,
    to_handle = target_user_handle
  )

# 2.2 Create edges from selected users to accounts they follow
edges_from_following <- all_following %>%
  transmute(
    from_did = source_user_did,
    to_did = did,
    from_handle = source_user_handle,
    to_handle = actor_handle
  )

# 2.3 Combine both types of edges
all_edges <- bind_rows(
  edges_from_followers,
  edges_from_following
)

# 2.4 Remove duplicate directed edges
all_edges <- all_edges %>%
  distinct(from_did, to_did, .keep_all = TRUE)

# 2.5 Inspect edge list
cat("Total unique edges:", nrow(all_edges), "\n")
print(head(all_edges, 10))
```

### 3. Create node list

```{r}
nodes_from <- all_edges %>%
  select(did = from_did, handle = from_handle)

nodes_to <- all_edges %>%
  select(did = to_did, handle = to_handle)

all_nodes <- bind_rows(nodes_from, nodes_to) %>%
  distinct(did, .keep_all = TRUE)

cat("Total unique nodes:", nrow(all_nodes), "\n")

# Identify the three selected users
all_nodes <- all_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    selected_user = did %in% top3_users$author_did
  )

print(all_nodes %>% count(selected_user))
```

### 4. Create directed network graph

```{r}
# Prepare edge data
graph_edges <- all_edges %>%
  transmute(
    from = from_did,
    to = to_did
  )

# Prepare vertex data
graph_nodes <- all_nodes %>%
  transmute(
    name = did,
    handle = handle,
    selected_user = selected_user
  )

# Create directed graph
network_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(
  d = graph_edges,
  directed = TRUE,
  vertices = graph_nodes
)

# Check graph information
cat("Number of vertices:", vcount(network_graph), "\n")
cat("Number of edges:", ecount(network_graph), "\n")
cat("Is directed:", is_directed(network_graph), "\n")
```

## Question 4C: Network Centrality and PageRank

### 1. Calculate centrality metrics

```{r}
in_degree <- degree(network_graph, mode = "in", normalized = TRUE)

out_degree <- degree(network_graph, mode = "out", normalized = TRUE)

pagerank_score <- page_rank(network_graph, directed = TRUE)$vector

# Combine results into one table
centrality_results <- data.frame(
  did = V(network_graph)$name,
  handle = V(network_graph)$handle,
  in_degree = as.numeric(in_degree),
  out_degree = as.numeric(out_degree),
  pagerank = as.numeric(pagerank_score)
)

head(centrality_results)

# Export the centrality result
write.csv(
  centrality_results,
  "q4c_centrality_result.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

### 2. Identify top users based on specific metrics

```{r}
# Top user by in-degree centrality
top_in_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  slice_max(order_by = in_degree, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
  select(handle, in_degree)

# Top user by out-degree centrality
top_out_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  slice_max(order_by = out_degree, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
  select(handle, out_degree)

# Top user by PageRank
top_pagerank <- centrality_results %>%
  slice_max(order_by = pagerank, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
  select(handle, pagerank)

# Display results
cat("Top user by In-degree Centrality:\n")
print(top_in_degree)

cat("Top user by Out-degree Centrality:\n")
print(top_out_degree)

cat("Top user by PageRank:\n")
print(top_pagerank)

# Export the result
write.csv(
  top_in_degree,
  "q4c_top_in_degree.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  top_out_degree,
  "q4c_top_out_degree.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  top_pagerank,
  "q4c_top_pagerank.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

**Centrality Analysis and Discussion**

- Three network centrality measures were calculated for all 202 nodes: in-degree centrality, out-degree centrality, and PageRank.

- In-degree centrality: The three selected users shared the highest in-degree centrality score of 0.2488. Each account had 50 incoming connections in the collected network, indicating that 50 collected accounts followed each selected user.

- Out-degree centrality: GameDropStation achieved the highest out-degree centrality score of 0.2239. This indicates that GameDropStation had the largest number of outgoing follow relationships within the collected network.

- PageRank: iGeek Gamer achieved the highest PageRank score of 0.1024. Although GameDropStation had the highest out-degree centrality, it did no achieve the highest PageRank score.

**Discussion: Degree Centrality versus PageRank**

- The result demonstrate that the degree centrality and PageRank measure different aspects of network structure.

- Degree centrality focuses on the number of direct connections a node has. For example, GameDropStation had the highest out-degree because it followed 46 accounts within the collected network.

- In contrast, PageRank considers not only the number of connections but also the importance of the nodes providing those connections. Therefore, a node can receive a higher PageRank score even if it does not have the highest degree.

- In this network, iGeek Gamer achieved the highest PageRank score (0.1025), despite having a lower out-degree that GameDropStation. This demonstrates that having more direct connections does not necessarily result in a higher PageRank score.
